paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is an autosomal recessive disorder in which the intestine selectively fails to absorb dietary glucose and galactose. It begins within the first weeks of life. The resulting severe diarrhea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991). The disorder is caused by a defect in the Na+/glucose cotransporter SGLT1 in the intestinal brush border (Turk et al., 1991; Martín et al., 1996).

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied intestinal and renal glucose transport in a 3-year-old girl with congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption and in her family. Her jejunal mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. In contrast, mucosa from 6 normal controls and from her asymptomatic 5-year-old brother accumulated glucose to 16 times its concentration in the incubation medium. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband. Her brother's titration curve was similar to those of 7 normal volunteers.

paragraphs.text: Abdullah et al. (1996) reported 8 Arab children from 8 different families with chronic diarrhea due to glucose-galactose malabsorption. Six were Saudi Arabs and 2 were of other Arab nationalities. Their mean age at presentation was 10.6 months. They presented with chronic watery diarrhea, present since birth, and failure to thrive. The diagnosis was confirmed by laboratory studies, including small-bowel biopsy, histology, and small-bowel enzyme assay. One child had a renal stone at the first visit, and a renal stone was found in another during follow-up. All of the children improved clinically on a fructose-based formula and were thriving at follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Xin and Wang (2011) reported 33 patients with GGM from a large Old Order Amish pedigree. All affected individuals presented with classic watery diarrhea and dehydration. Other initial findings included increased bowel sounds, a distended abdomen, vigorous nursing despite illness, irritability, and apathy. When patients were correctly diagnosed and adequately managed, the diarrhea stopped immediately and they rehydrated quickly, with normal growth and development afterward. When the disease was not recognized, the clinical course was prolonged.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. Both parents and a half sister of a proband with GGM had impaired glucose transport, with values between those of normal controls and those of the proband. Glucose influx was impaired in these 3 heterozygotes, but glucose efflux from their mucosa was the same as in 3 normal controls. Kinetic analysis showed reduced capacity (Vmax) but normal affinity (Km) for glucose transport in their intestinal mucosa. Fructose accumulation was similar in all subjects.

paragraphs.text: Turk et al. (1991) noted that intestinal biopsies from patients with GGM had shown a specific defect in Na+-dependent glucose absorption in the brush border. Normally, glucose is absorbed by the Na+/glucose cotransporter in the brush border membrane of the intestinal epithelium. Uptake into the cell is driven by the transmembrane Na+ electrochemical potential gradient, and the sugar then passes to the blood across the basolateral membrane via the facilitated glucose carrier. Martín et al. (1996) found that defects in both SGLT1 trafficking and SGLT1 function cause GGM.

paragraphs.text: Turk et al. (1991) noted that the severe diarrhea and dehydration of GGM are usually fatal unless glucose and galactose are removed from the diet. All 8 Arab children reported by Abdullah et al. (1996) improved clinically on a fructose-based formula. In the Amish patients reported by Xin and Wang (2011), correct diagnosis and adequate management stopped the diarrhea immediately and led to quick rehydration, followed by normal growth and development.

Death in infancy if glucose and galactose are not removed from diet

paragraphs.text: Turk et al. (1991) found a missense mutation in the SGLT1 gene in a family with GGM. The mutation cosegregated with the phenotype and caused complete loss of Na+-dependent glucose transport when expressed in Xenopus oocytes. Turk et al. (1993) identified this change as asp28-to-asn (D28N), found in 2 patients with GGM, and noted that it abolished SGLT1 transport activity in vitro.

checks.evidence_quote: Sequence analysis of the amplified products has revealed a single missense mutation in SGLT1 which cosegregates with the GGM phenotype
checks.explanation: The abstract reports this mutation in a family affected with GGM.

paragraphs.text: Martín et al. (1996) reported that 2 proband sibs with GGM from a large consanguineous family carried the D28N mutation. In prenatal testing by EcoRV restriction digestion of PCR-amplified exon 1, a later sib was heterozygous and a cousin was not a carrier. Both remained healthy at 2 years of age.

paragraphs.text: In 33 patients with GGM from a large Old Order Amish pedigree, Xin and Wang (2011) found a homozygous c.152A-G transition in the SLC5A1 gene, resulting in an asn51-to-ser (N51S) substitution. The variant was found by sequencing the coding exons and exon-intron boundaries. It cosegregated with GGM in all affected individuals, together with 3 other homozygous missense variants: A411T, R558H, and H615Q.
